meta.title: Along a String, Not Across the Neck
meta.summary: Drop the five-fret window as the unit entirely: one octave along a single string passes through all five CAGED forms in order, and a string pair plays the same journey in four notes each.

spans.text: The Note That Belongs to Both
kept the window and added a door in it. This lesson throws the window away. The unit is not a five-fret box anymore. It is a single string.
Play
C
major on the low E string and nothing else — no other string, no window boundary to respect. The scale falls at frets
, and each one sits inside whichever window happens to contain that fret.
Those eight notes pass through all five windows, in
C-A-G-E-D

order, once. An octave on one string is twelve frets. The five windows tile twelve frets. So one octave along a single string is exactly one full turn of the wheel — every window, in order, without ever choosing one to stay inside. You cannot be boxed in on a string, because a string has no box to be in.
The high e string reads identically, fret for fret, because strings 6 and 1 are two octaves apart at the same fret — chapter 1's cheapest fact, still true and still useful.

Say plainly what this costs. Twelve frets is a long stretch for one hand, and getting there means a lot of position shifting for very little musical payoff — nobody plays a whole solo up one string. What it buys instead is a rewiring of how the neck looks: where the
falls on each string, where the half-steps are hiding, and that map is exactly what makes the version people actually play readable.
The version people actually play uses a pair of strings instead of one — four notes on the lower string, four on the next one up, one full octave between them.

The pattern on the next string up is the same four frets, moved. Crossing from string 5 to string 4 the shift is two frets, matching chapter 1's rule for the
and
octave jumps. Crossing from string 3 to string 2 the shift is three frets instead, because
G → B
is the one major third hiding in standard tuning — the same irregularity, showing up again as a horizontal move instead of a vertical one. Run it on strings 3 and 2 and you feel the extra fret:
, then
Where the
run starts and stops matters. It begins on
— a root, and the doorway between the C and A windows. It ends on

— a root, and the doorway between the E and D windows. Do not mistake this for a run that climbs steadily through the five windows: crossing from string 5 to string 4 steps back three frets, from fret 8 down to fret 5. The honest claim is smaller and still striking — the run travels from fret 3 to fret 10 and never settles inside any one window on the way.
Four notes on one string, then the same four notes moved up two frets on the next. Moved up three instead, the one time the crossing is string 3 to string 2.
Open the
Drone
on
C
. Run the low E string first, then the

pair, against that sustained root. A line moving up the neck sounds like it is going somewhere, in a way a line moving across the strings at one fret range never quite does — and now you know exactly why: one is walking through all five windows, and the other is standing still inside one of them.
Scale Visualizer
will trace either journey for you, live, if you'd rather watch it than count frets.
A Progression Without Going Back to the Nut
